t.2.50.1: Then, when the night had passed, Raghunandana gently awakened Lakṣmaṇa, who lay asleep close beside him.
t.2.50.3: Lakṣmaṇa, who had been sleeping, was awakened at the proper time by his brother, and he cast off his sleep and drowsiness and the weariness that had clung to him on the road.
t.2.50.2: Saumitri, listen to the sound of the forest creatures calling sweetly. Let us set out, O scorcher of foes; it is time for departure.
t.2.50.4: Then they all rose, and having touched the auspicious water of the river, they set out on that path to Citrakūṭa which the sage had pointed out.
t.2.50.5: Then Rāma, having set out at the proper time together with Saumitri, spoke these words to Sītā, whose eyes were like lotus petals.
t.2.50.6: O Vaidehī, behold the kiṃśuka trees, blossoming everywhere now that the cool season has passed, garlanded with their own flowers as though ablaze.
t.2.50.7: Look at the bhallātaka trees in full bloom, untouched by men, bent low with fruit and leaves; surely I shall be able to live here.
t.2.50.8: Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the honey hanging down on every tree, in masses as large as a droṇa, gathered by the bees.
t.2.50.9: Here the natyūha bird cries out, and the peacock calls back in answer, in this lovely stretch of forest crowded with carpets of flowers.
t.2.50.10: Behold this mountain Citrakūṭa with its lofty peaks, frequented by herds of elephants and resounding with the cries of flocks of birds.
t.2.50.11: Then the two of them, going on foot together with Sītā, reached the lovely mountain Citrakūṭa, delightful to the mind.
t.2.50.13: Lakṣmaṇa, bring wood, both strong and choice, and build a dwelling, gentle one, for my mind delights in living here.
t.2.50.12: Having reached that mountain, thronged with flocks of many kinds of birds, let this be our dwelling for the present; here, gentle one, let us take our delight.
t.2.50.14: Hearing those words of his, Saumitri, the subduer of foes, brought trees of many kinds, and then he built a hut of leaves.
t.2.50.15: He spoke these words to him, who was attentive and eager to serve: “Having brought the meat of a black antelope, we shall consecrate the hut with a sacrifice.”
t.2.50.16: That valiant Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, having slain a black antelope fit for sacrifice, then cast it into the blazing fire.
t.2.50.17: Perceiving that it was cooked, thoroughly roasted, its blood drained away, Lakṣmaṇa then spoke to Rāghava, the tiger among men.
t.2.50.18: This black antelope, whole in all its limbs, has been cooked just as it should be. O you who are like a god, worship the deities, for you are skilled in this.
t.2.50.19: Rāma, having bathed, self-restrained and virtuous, skilled in sacred recitation, then made an excellent offering that removes sin.
t.2.50.21: In that finest of forests, thronged with many and various beasts and birds, filled with trees bearing clusters of many-coloured blossoms, and resounding with the cries of beasts of prey, they who had mastered their senses roamed about most happily.
t.2.50.20: All of them together entered that charming hut, roofed with the leaves of trees, well built to suit its site and sheltered from the wind, to dwell there, just as the hosts of gods enter the assembly hall Sudharmā.
t.2.50.22: Having reached the most delightful Citrakūṭa and that river Mālyavatī with its fine fords, frequented by beasts and birds, he rejoiced, thrilled with joy, and cast off the sorrow born of his exile from the city.
